entry.title: Bitcoin Core v32.1 Released
entry.summary:
Bitcoin Core version 32.1 has been released, superseding the unpublished 32.0 release. This new version brings a wealth of features, bug fixes, performance enhancements, and updated translations. Users are encouraged to download it from [bitcoin-core-32.1](https://bitcoincore.org/bin/bitcoin-core-32.1/), and report issues via the [GitHub issue tracker](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues). With this release, support for versions 29.x and earlier has ended, meaning these older versions will not receive further updates.
Upgrading to 32.1 is straightforward and compatible with previous wallet formats. Users should properly shut down their existing Bitcoin Core instance before installing or copying over the new binaries. Direct upgrades from end-of-life (EOL) versions are supported but may require additional time if data migration is needed. The software remains officially supported on Linux Kernel 3.17+, macOS 14+, and Windows 10 (version 1903+), though it may function on other Unix-like systems without formal testing.
Several significant changes have been made to peer-to-peer networking and transaction relay mechanisms. Tor hidden services created by Bitcoin Core now enable [proof-of-work defenses](https://tpo.pages.torproject.net/onion-services/ecosystem/technology/security/pow/) when supported by the Tor daemon, enhancing network security. Transaction relay rate-limiting has shifted from per-peer to a global backlog model, reducing resource consumption during heavy transaction periods. Outgoing transaction bandwidth is now also limited, with key parameters accessible via RPC. Notably, a potential leak of a sender’s IP address through the `sendrawtransaction` RPC in certain Tor configurations has been fixed, ensuring privacy is preserved even in edge cases involving protocol downgrades. The private broadcast queue for transactions is now capped to prevent overload, and each transaction sent privately is restricted to 1,000 send attempts. Support for legacy ElGamal encryption in I2P is being phased out, and discussion is underway regarding the possible removal of CJDNS support due to low adoption.
Connection limits have been revised: the default maximum number of automatic peer connections has increased from 125 to 200, with configurable inbound transaction-relay slots. Automatic outbound connection numbers remain unchanged, and explicit `-maxconnections` values are still respected, with safeguards against excessively high settings.
Mempool-related RPCs have been updated for clarity and consistency. Deprecated fields such as `fullrbf` and `bip125-replaceable` are now only available if specifically requested, reflecting the long-standing defaults. New and updated RPC commands expand the flexibility and transparency of node operations: PSBT-related RPCs default to version 2 and allow explicit version selection; debug information about non-standard transaction inputs is now included in relevant RPC responses and logs; and mempool statistics are enhanced with the introduction of two distinct fee rate estimators—one block-based and one mempool-based—whose results are combined for smarter fee recommendations. The `estimatesmartfee` command now supports multiple estimator modes and provides detailed mempool health statistics when requested.
Additional improvements in RPC functionality include support for UNIX named pipes in `dumptxoutset`, more accurate reporting of blockchain validation progress, and new fields in balance-related RPCs to account for transactions excluded from the mempool. RPC configuration has been streamlined, removing deprecated options such as `-deprecatedrpc=startingheight`, and extending error handling for features like private broadcasts.
Newly added RPCs provide greater introspection and automation capabilities. The `exportasmap` RPC enables export of ASMap data used for IP address clustering, while `getopenrpcinfo` delivers a machine-readable OpenRPC description of all available RPC methods, facilitating advanced integrations and documentation.
On the build system front, future releases will discontinue official support for building with MSVC once clang-cl is ready. Git metadata detection has been improved for builds from source archives. Logging categories have been refined—such as the addition of a mining-specific category—and the HTTP server now enforces stricter compliance with RFC standards thanks to a custom implementation replacing Libevent.
Wallet management sees several noteworthy upgrades. A new RPC, `addhdkey`, allows direct addition of BIP 32 extended keys. Another new RPC, `exportwatchonlywallet`, creates a watch-only wallet file without private keys, streamlining offline signing workflows. The `derivehdkey` RPC facilitates complex multisig setups by deriving xpubs or xprvs along specific hardened paths. Wallet naming restrictions have been tightened for security, and experimental status has been lifted from the `send` and `sendall` RPCs. Certain deprecated wallet features, like `removeprunedfunds`, are scheduled for removal in future releases. Security has also been enhanced around wallet notification handling, preventing potential command injection through crafted wallet names.
The graphical user interface has been updated to Qt 6.8.
